claim: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters constitute the largest family of primary active transporters involved in a multitude of physiological processes and human diseases.
source: ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters constitute the largest family of primary active transporters involved in a multitude of physiological processes and human diseases.
evidence: This is a general statement about ABC transporters that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: High-affinity peptidic macrocycles bind conformationally selective and display potent multimode inhibitory effects.
source: High-affinity peptidic macrocycles bind conformationally selective and display potent multimode inhibitory effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including binding assays and inhibition studies.

claim: The macrocycles block the transporter either before or after unidirectional substrate export along a single conformational switch induced by ATP binding.
source: The macrocycles block the transporter either before or after unidirectional substrate export along a single conformational switch induced by ATP binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleotide occlusion assays and single-liposome transport studies.

claim: ABC transporters are implicated in cystic fibrosis.
source: They are implicated in many physiological processes and diseases including cystic fibrosis (Stutts et al., 1995; Csanády et al., 2019), diabetes (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999), lipid-trafficking disorders (Brooks-Wilson et al., 1999), antibiotic resistance (Orelle et al., 2019), and acquired drug resistance in cancer chemotherapy (Kartner et al., 1983; Litman et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ABC transporters are implicated in diabetes.
source: They are implicated in many physiological processes and diseases including cystic fibrosis (Stutts et al., 1995; Csanády et al., 2019), diabetes (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999), lipid-trafficking disorders (Brooks-Wilson et al., 1999), antibiotic resistance (Orelle et al., 2019), and acquired drug resistance in cancer chemotherapy (Kartner et al., 1983; Litman et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ABC transporters are implicated in lipid-trafficking disorders.
source: They are implicated in many physiological processes and diseases including cystic fibrosis (Stutts et al., 1995; Csanády et al., 2019), diabetes (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999), lipid-trafficking disorders (Brooks-Wilson et al., 1999), antibiotic resistance (Orelle et al., 2019), and acquired drug resistance in cancer chemotherapy (Kartner et al., 1983; Litman et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ABC transporters are implicated in antibiotic resistance.
source: They are implicated in many physiological processes and diseases including cystic fibrosis (Stutts et al., 1995; Csanády et al., 2019), diabetes (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999), lipid-trafficking disorders (Brooks-Wilson et al., 1999), antibiotic resistance (Orelle et al., 2019), and acquired drug resistance in cancer chemotherapy (Kartner et al., 1983; Litman et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ABC transporters are implicated in acquired drug resistance in cancer chemotherapy.
source: They are implicated in many physiological processes and diseases including cystic fibrosis (Stutts et al., 1995; Csanády et al., 2019), diabetes (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999), lipid-trafficking disorders (Brooks-Wilson et al., 1999), antibiotic resistance (Orelle et al., 2019), and acquired drug resistance in cancer chemotherapy (Kartner et al., 1983; Litman et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ABC transporters are composed of two transmembrane domains (TMDs), forming the substrate translocation pathway, and two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs), converting the chemical energy of ATP binding and hydrolysis into mechanic transitions.
source: ABC transporters are composed of two transmembrane domains (TMDs), forming the substrate translocation pathway, and two nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs), converting the chemical energy of ATP binding and hydrolysis into mechanic transitions (Rees et al., 2009; Locher, 2016; Thomas and Tampé, 2018; Oldham et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The heterodimeric multidrug resistance transporter TmrAB from Thermus thermophilus shares structural and functional homology with the transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP).
source: The heterodimeric multidrug resistance transporter TmrAB from Thermus thermophilus shares structural and functional homology with the transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP) and can restore antigen presentation in human TAP-deficient cells (Kim et al., 2015; Nöll et al., 2017; Zutz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TmrAB can restore antigen presentation in human TAP-deficient cells.
source: The heterodimeric multidrug resistance transporter TmrAB from Thermus thermophilus shares structural and functional homology with the transporter associated with antigen processing (TAP) and can restore antigen presentation in human TAP-deficient cells (Kim et al., 2015; Nöll et al., 2017; Zutz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TmrAB is particularly suitable for mechanistic and structural studies, as the various conformers along the translocation trajectory are only accessible at elevated temperatures.
source: TmrAB is particularly suitable for mechanistic and structural studies, as the various conformers along the translocation trajectory are only accessible at elevated temperatures, thus providing active control over the system (Nöll et al., 2017; Zutz et al., 2011; Hofmann et al., 2019; Stefan et al., 2020; Barth et al., 2018; Barth et al., 2020; Diederichs and Tampé, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Several catalytic models for ABC systems have been depicted including alternating sites, constant contact, and processive clamp/ATP switch.
source: To correlate ATP binding and hydrolysis to substrate transport, several catalytic models for ABC systems have been depicted including alternating sites (Senior et al., 1995), constant contact (Jones and George, 2009), and processive clamp/ATP switch (Higgins and Linton, 2004; Janas et al., 2003; Abele and Tampé, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In all models, substrate translocation is coupled with conformational transitions, which are linked to the ATP hydrolysis cycle.
source: In all models, substrate translocation is coupled with conformational transitions, which are linked to the ATP hydrolysis cycle (Thomas and Tampé, 2020; Szöllősi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The conformational landscape of a heterodimeric ABC transporter has recently been elucidated through nine high-resolution X-ray and cryo-EM structures.
source: The conformational landscape of a heterodimeric ABC transporter has recently been elucidated through nine high-resolution X-ray and cryo-EM structures (Nöll et al., 2017; Hofmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Using single liposome-based translocation assays, the unidirectional substrate export along a single conformational switch induced by ATP binding was demonstrated.
source: Using single liposome-based translocation assays, the unidirectional substrate export along a single conformational switch induced by ATP binding was demonstrated (Stefan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Many bioactive toxins, antibiotics, and inhibitors are macrocyclic peptides (CPs) with unnatural amino acid modifications.
source: Many bioactive toxins, antibiotics, and inhibitors are macrocyclic peptides (CPs) with unnatural amino acid modifications (Nicolaou et al., 1999; Obexer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CPs are regarded as next-generation pharmaceutical compounds to target 'undruggable' proteins implicated in disease and diagnosis.
source: CPs are regarded as next-generation pharmaceutical compounds to target 'undruggable' proteins implicated in disease and diagnosis (Morrison, 2018; Vinogradov et al., 2019; Zorzi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Various engineered and modified CPs are clinically approved or under clinical trials, for example, Peginesatide, Linaclotide, and Pasireotide.
source: To this end, various engineered and modified CPs are clinically approved or under clinical trials, for example, Peginesatide, Linaclotide, and Pasireotide.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about approved pharmaceutical compounds.

claim: Compared to conventional small-molecule drugs, CPs usually display an elevated selectivity as well as an increased potency, and they are easy to manufacture.
source: Compared to conventional small-molecule drugs, CPs usually display an elevated selectivity as well as an increased potency, and they are easy to manufacture (Craik et al., 2013; Driggers et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The random nonstandard peptide integrated discovery (RaPID) system comprises the identification of synthetic/de novo CPs against desired target protein complexes to enable structural and functional investigations.
source: The random nonstandard peptide integrated discovery (RaPID) system comprises the identification of synthetic/de novo CPs against desired target protein complexes to enable structural and functional investigations (Murakami et al., 2006a; Murakami et al., 2006b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Unnatural amino acids such as N-chloroacetyl-d-tyrosine, N-methyl alanine, and carboranyl alanine can be incorporated by the Flexible In-vitro Translation (FIT) system.
source: As a major advantage, unnatural amino acids such as N-chloroacetyl-d-tyrosine (Goto et al., 2008), N-methyl alanine (Yamagishi et al., 2011), and carboranyl alanine (Yin et al., 2019) can be incorporated by the Flexible In-vitro Translation (FIT) system, relying on aminoacylating ribozymes called Flexizymes (Goto et al., 2011) to construct highly diverse peptide libraries.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Using the RaPID system, CPs were identified for receptor tyrosine kinases, ubiquitin ligase, the Zika virus protease, prolyl hydroxylase, and phosphoglycerate mutases.
source: Using the RaPID system, CPs were identified for receptor tyrosine kinases (Yin et al., 2019), ubiquitin ligase (Yamagishi et al., 2011), the Zika virus protease (Nitsche et al., 2019), prolyl hydroxylase (McAllister et al., 2018), and phosphoglycerate mutases (Yu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Enriched CPs specifically bind to TmrAB and are high-affinity allosteric inhibitors, which prevent substrate transport and ATP turnover.
source: Enriched CPs specifically bind to TmrAB and are high-affinity allosteric inhibitors, which prevent substrate transport and ATP turnover.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from binding assays, transport assays, and ATPase assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two mechanistically distinct CP inhibitor classes were elucidated that arrest the ABC transporter either before or right after ATP-binding induced substrate translocation.
source: Two mechanistically distinct CP inhibitor classes were elucidated that arrest the ABC transporter either before or right after ATP-binding induced substrate translocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from nucleotide occlusion and transport assays.

claim: These CPs arrest TmrAB in the inward-facing (IF) and outward-facing conformation, respectively.
source: Thus, these CPs arrest TmrAB in the inward-facing (IF) and outward-facing conformation, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from conformation-specific binding studies.

claim: The final library size was on the order of 10^12 macrocyclic peptides.
source: The final library size was on the order of 1012 macrocyclic peptides.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods used to generate the library.

claim: Head-to-side chain cyclization was mediated through ribosomal incorporation of N-chloroacetyl-d-tyrosine at the initiator position, which post-translationally undergoes intramolecular thioether formation with a downstream cysteine.
source: Head-to-side chain cyclization was mediated through ribosomal incorporation of N-chloroacetyl-d-tyrosine at the initiator position, which post-translationally undergoes intramolecular thioether formation with a downstream cysteine (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: After five iterative rounds of selection, including in vitro translation, affinity panning, reverse transcription, and PCR recovery, high-affinity binders were identified by deep sequencing.
source: After five iterative rounds of selection, including in vitro translation, affinity panning, reverse transcription, and PCR recovery, high-affinity binders were identified by deep sequencing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental methods described.

claim: The most abundant macrocyclic peptides after the fifth selection round, CP6, CP12, CP13, and CP14, constituted 41% of the final sequenced pool.
source: The most abundant macrocyclic peptides after the fifth selection round, CP6, CP12, CP13, and CP14, constituted 41% of the final sequenced pool and could not be grouped into families (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All CPFs bind to TmrAB with nanomolar binding affinities, with KD values ranging from 20 to 50 nM.
source: The equilibrium binding revealed nanomolar binding affinities for all CPFs, with KD values ranging from 20 to 50 nM (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: If empty liposomes (without reconstituted TmrAB) were added to CPFs, no binding was detected, demonstrating a specific interaction of all CPs with TmrAB.
source: If empty liposomes (without reconstituted TmrAB) were added to CPFs, no binding was detected, demonstrating a specific interaction of all CPs with TmrAB (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: TmrAB complexes could be affinity-captured on streptavidin beads pre-loaded with biotinylated CPBs.
source: Notably, TmrAB complexes could be affinity-captured on streptavidin beads pre-loaded with biotinylated CPBs and detected in the eluate but not in the flow-through (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by affinity capture data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CP13B and CP14B immobilized on streptavidin matrices can isolate intact TmrAB complexes from solubilized E. coli membranes.
source: To explore the specificity of binding, we used CP13B and CP14B immobilized on streptavidin matrices to isolate intact TmrAB complexes from solubilized E. coli membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by affinity purification data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: For all CPFs, kinetically stable CPF-TmrAB complexes were formed as confirmed by gel filtration.
source: For all CPFs, kinetically stable CPF-TmrAB complexes were formed as confirmed by gel filtration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under conditions where the quaternary and tertiary structure of TmrAB complexes is disrupted by adding anionic detergent SDS, binding of TmrAB to all CPFs was impaired, indicating a conformation-specific interaction.
source: To address whether the CPs recognize a linear or non-linear epitope, we examined the binding of CPFs after disrupting the quaternary and tertiary structure of TmrAB complexes by adding anionic detergent SDS. Under these conditions, binding of TmrAB to all CPFs was impaired, indicating a conformation-specific interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Native mass spectrometry demonstrates a stoichiometric interaction between CPFs and TmrAB.
source: We also analyzed the CPF-TmrAB complexes by native mass spectrometry (MS), demonstrating a stoichiometric interaction (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by native MS data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the presence of the CPFs, ATPase activity was completely blocked to the level of autohydrolysis.
source: In the presence of the CPFs, ATPase activity was completely blocked to the level of autohydrolysis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATPase activity data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: None of the CPFs were transported by TmrAB.
source: In contrast to the linear substrate peptide C4F, none of the CPFs were transported by TmrAB (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by transport assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CP6F and CP12F completely blocked peptide translocation.
source: The data reveal that CP6F and CP12F completely blocked peptide translocation, while CP13F or CP14F only caused a partial inhibition (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by transport assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CP13F or CP14F only caused a partial inhibition of peptide translocation.
source: The data reveal that CP6F and CP12F completely blocked peptide translocation, while CP13F or CP14F only caused a partial inhibition (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by transport assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At competitive concentrations above their KD values, the transported peptides R9LQK or C4ATTO655 did not affect binding of CPFs to TmrAB.
source: At competitive concentrations above their KD values (Stefan et al., 2020), the transported peptides R9LQK or C4ATTO655 did not affect binding of CPFs to TmrAB (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by competition binding data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CPBs as competitors did not affect C4F peptide binding, in contrast to the linear peptide C4ATTO655, which interfered with C4F peptide binding.
source: In the second inverse approach using CPBs as competitors, we did not observe a competition of C4F peptide binding, in contrast to the linear peptide C4ATTO655, which interfered with C4F peptide binding (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by competition binding data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CP12B and CP14B showed no effect on ATP binding.
source: CP12B and CP14B showed no effect on ATP binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by scintillation proximity assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For CP6B and CP13B, only minor effects on ATP binding were detected.
source: For CP6B and CP13B, only minor effects on ATP binding were detected (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by scintillation proximity assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CPs are high-affinity allosteric inhibitors of TmrAB that leave ATP binding and substrate interaction largely unaffected, while impairing ATP hydrolysis and substrate translocation across the membrane.
source: Taken together, CPs are high-affinity allosteric inhibitors of TmrAB that leave ATP binding and substrate interaction largely unaffected, while impairing ATP hydrolysis and substrate translocation across the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data including binding assays, ATPase assays, and transport assays.

claim: Binding of CP6F and CP12F showed lower dissociation constants for the OF conformation in contrast to CP13F and CP14F, which show a preference for the OF conformer.
source: Binding of CP6F and CP12F showed lower dissociation constants for the OF conformation in contrast to CP13F and CP14F, which show a preference for the OF conformer (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by conformation-specific binding data shown in Figure 5A, B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CP13F and CP14F bind in the absence and presence of ATP and ADP, while CP6F and CP12F preferentially bind under conditions where IF TmrAB is exclusively populated.
source: These findings were further corroborated by demonstrating that CP13F and CP14F bind in the absence and presence of ATP and ADP, while CP6F and CP12F preferentially bind under conditions where IF TmrAB is exclusively populated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by binding data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the presence of CP6F and CP12F, nucleotide occlusion was completely abolished.
source: In the presence of CP6F and CP12F, nucleotide occlusion was completely abolished.
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide occlusion data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: CP13F and CP14F promoted stable ATP occlusion in wild-type TmrAB – blocking hydrolysis to ADP, which is indicative of stabilization of a pre-hydrolysis state.
source: Notably, CP13F and CP14F promoted stable ATP occlusion in wild-type TmrAB – blocking hydrolysis to ADP, which is indicative of stabilization of a pre-hydrolysis state (Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by nucleotide occlusion data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: CP6F and CP12F display preferential binding to the IF conformation and inhibit the IF-to-OF switch by ATP binding.
source: In conclusion, CP6F and CP12F display preferential binding to the IF conformation and inhibit the IF-to-OF switch by ATP binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by conformation-specific binding and nucleotide occlusion data.

claim: CP13F and CP14F favorably bind to the OF conformation, promoting ATP occlusion, thus stabilizing TmrAB in a pre-hydrolysis state.
source: In contrast, CP13F and CP14F favorably bind to the OF conformation, promoting ATP occlusion, thus stabilizing TmrAB in a pre-hydrolysis state.
evidence: This claim is supported by conformation-specific binding and nucleotide occlusion data.

claim: Along a single IF-to-OF switch and arrest by CP13F or CP14F, approx. 10 or 30 C4ATTO655 peptides per liposome were transported, respectively.
source: Along a single IF-to-OF switch and arrest by CP13F or CP14F, approx. 10 or 30 C4ATTO655 peptides per liposome were transported, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-liposome flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A coupling ratio of 0.3 to 1.0 peptides per transporter along the ATP-induced IF-to-OF switch can be derived.
source: From that, a coupling ratio of 0.3 to 1.0 peptides per transporter along the ATP-induced IF-to-OF switch can be derived.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the transport data and the number of transporters per liposome.

claim: CP6F and CP12F completely prevented C4ATTO655 peptide translocation.
source: In contrast, CP6F and CP12F completely prevented C4ATTO655 peptide translocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-liposome flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The binding epitope of all CPs is on the TmrAB regions facing the cytosol.
source: Taking into account that the CPs are membrane impermeable, these results indicate that the binding epitope of all CPs is on the TmrAB regions facing the cytosol.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the membrane impermeability of CPs and their ability to inhibit transport.

claim: Compared to the positive control in the absence of CPFs, CP13F and CP14F drastically reduced the peptide transport rate.
source: Compared to the positive control in the absence of CPFs, CP13F and CP14F drastically reduced the peptide transport rate (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course transport data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: For CP13F, a single turnover driving peptide transport was observed before wild-type TmrAB became conformationally arrested.
source: For CP13F, a single turnover driving peptide transport was observed before wild-type TmrAB became conformationally arrested (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course transport data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the presence of CP14F, a slow turnover of wild-type TmrAB driving peptide transport over a period of 40 min was noted.
source: In the presence of CP14F, we noted a slow turnover of wild-type TmrAB driving peptide transport over a period of 40 min (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course transport data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: In the presence of CP13F, peptide transport was exclusively observed along the first IF-to-OF switch, indicating a conformational arrest of wild-type TmrAB over a period of 2 hr.
source: In the presence of CP13F, peptide transport was exclusively observed along the first IF-to-OF switch, indicating a conformational arrest of wild-type TmrAB over a period of 2 hr (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-cycle transport data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: For CP14F, peptide transport was detected in both IF-to-OF switches, which confirmed the slow relaxation of wild-type TmrAB from a pre-hydrolysis to an IF state between both cycles.
source: For CP14F, peptide transport was detected in both IF-to-OF switches, which confirmed the slow relaxation of wild-type TmrAB from a pre-hydrolysis to an IF state between both cycles (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-cycle transport data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The macrocyclic peptides CP13 and CP14 stabilize a pre-hydrolysis state, thus allowing a single-turnover translocation along the IF-to-OF switch.
source: Taken together, the macrocyclic peptides CP13 and CP14 stabilize a pre-hydrolysis state, thus allowing a single-turnover translocation along the IF-to-OF switch.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental data including nucleotide occlusion and transport assays.

claim: Macrocyclic peptides can be employed to arrest TmrAB at different stages during a single IF-to-OF switch induced by ATP binding, which drives substrate transport across the membrane.
source: We reveal that CPs can be employed to arrest TmrAB at different stages during a single IF-to-OF switch induced by ATP binding, which drives substrate transport across the membrane (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: These IF-to-OF and OF-to-IF inhibitors stabilize TmrAB states that are distinct from the vanadate trapped states.
source: These IF-to-OF and OF-to-IF inhibitors stabilize TmrAB states that are distinct from the vanadate trapped states and allowed us to unravel mechanistic principles of substrate transport for wild-type ABC transproters and illustrate the potential of selective inhibitors as next-generation antibiotics.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of nucleotide occlusion patterns between CP-arrested and vanadate-trapped states.

claim: CPs are powerful agents to stabilize protein conformers or protein complexes for structural and functional investigations.
source: It has been shown that CPs are powerful agents to stabilize protein conformers or protein complexes for structural and functional investigations (Huang et al., 2019; Passioura and Suga, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Upon cyclization of the peptide backbone, CPs mimic the complementary-determining regions (CDRs) of antibodies penetrating into buried cavities.
source: Upon cyclization of the peptide backbone, CPs mimic the complementary-determining regions (CDRs) of antibodies penetrating into buried cavities (Hill et al., 2014; McGeary and Fairlie, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Compared to conventional antibodies and antibody fragments, the incorporation of unnatural amino acids largely expands the chemical diversity of paratopes to reach unexplored binding modes.
source: Compared to conventional antibodies and antibody fragments, the incorporation of unnatural amino acids largely expands the chemical diversity of paratopes to reach unexplored binding modes (Craik et al., 2013; Makley and Gestwicki, 2013; Tsomaia, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: All CPs selected against TmrAEQB in lipid nanodiscs also specifically bind to wild-type TmrAB in various lipid models.
source: As demonstrated by affinity isolation, gel filtration, and native mass spectrometry, all CPs selected against TmrAEQB in lipid nanodiscs also specifically bind to wild-type TmrAB in various lipid models.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from affinity isolation, gel filtration, and native MS.

claim: The most enriched macrocyclic peptides also display inhibitory activity, even though the selection is based on target binding alone.
source: Intriguingly, the most enriched macrocyclic peptides also display inhibitory activity, even though the selection is based on target binding alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that enriched CPs inhibit ATPase activity and transport.

claim: Based on deep sequencing, CP6 and CP12, acting on the IF state, showed higher enrichment than CP13 and CP14, acting on the OF state, which is consistent with the selections being performed at 4°C, where TmrAB adopts the IF state.
source: Based on deep sequencing, CP6 and CP12, acting on the IF state, showed higher enrichment than CP13 and CP14, acting on the OF state, which is consistent with the selections being performed at 4°C, where TmrAB adopts the IF state.
evidence: This claim is supported by deep sequencing data and the known conformational preference of TmrAB at different temperatures.

claim: Due to high binding affinities of OF-specific CP13 and CP14, these CPs were also enriched along the course of the selection.
source: However, due to high binding affinities of OF-specific CP13 and CP14, these CPs were also enriched along the course of the selection.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the enrichment data and binding affinities.

claim: In contrast to CPs elicited against the homodimeric ABC transporter cmABCB1 from Cyanidioschyzon merolae (aCAP) and the MATE transporter (MaD3S, MaD5, MaL6), the CPs discovered in this study exclusively target the transporter from the cytosolic side.
source: In contrast to CPs elicited against the homodimeric ABC transporter cmABCB1 from Cyanidioschyzon merolae (aCAP) (Kodan et al., 2014) and the MATE transporter (MaD3S, MaD5, MaL6) (Tanaka et al., 2013), the CPs discovered in this study exclusively target the transporter from the cytosolic side.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the membrane impermeability of CPs and comparison with other studies.

claim: In the case of aCAP, which was selected against detergent stabilized P-glycoprotein, the CP not only interacts with both protein subunits but also with the membrane, acting as an allosteric inhibitor thus stabilizing this ABC transporter in the IF conformation.
source: In the case of aCAP, which was selected against detergent stabilized P-glycoprotein, the CP not only interacts with both protein subunits but also with the membrane, acting as an allosteric inhibitor thus stabilizing this ABC transporter in the IF conformation.
evidence: This claim is based on prior research on aCAP.

claim: Like aCAP, the CPs from this study are also enriched in aliphatic and aromatic amino acids, which could indicate membrane interactions.
source: Like aCAP, the CPs from this study are also enriched in aliphatic and aromatic amino acids, which could indicate membrane interactions.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and speculation about potential membrane interactions.

claim: The ability of the CP6, CP12, CP13, and CP14 to specifically interact with either the IF or OF TmrAB conformer suggests that the success of this selection experiment in discovering multimode inhibitors relied on specific preparation of the bait protein during the selection process.
source: The ability of the CP6, CP12, CP13, and CP14 to specifically interact with either the IF or OF TmrAB conformer however, again suggests that the success of this selection experiment in discovering multimode inhibitors relied on specific preparation of the bait protein during the selection process.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the conformation-specific binding of CPs.

claim: In recent years, the molecular understanding of the conformation space of ABC transporters has been largely expanded.
source: In recent years, the molecular understanding of the conformation space of ABC transporters has been largely expanded (Thomas and Tampé, 2020; Locher, 2016; Hofmann et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: High-resolution structures in different conformational states allowed to build a detailed mechanistic model of the substrate transport cycle composed of two major conformational transitions (IF-to-OF and OF-to-IF).
source: High-resolution structures in different conformational states allowed to build a detailed mechanistic model of the substrate transport cycle composed of two major conformational transitions (IF-to-OF and OF-to-IF) (Hofmann et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2020; Manolaridis et al., 2018; Kim and Chen, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Unidirectional substrate transport along a single IF-to-OF switch induced by ATP binding was demonstrated for a catalytically reduced variant of TmrAB.
source: We demonstrated unidirectional substrate transport along a single IF-to-OF switch induced by ATP binding for a catalytically reduced variant of TmrAB (Stefan et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: These results were consistent with the processive-clamp/ATP switch model where ATP binding and the subsequent IF-to-OF switch represent the power stroke to drive substrate transport.
source: These results were consistent with the processive-clamp/ATP switch model where ATP binding and the subsequent IF-to-OF switch represent the power stroke to drive substrate transport (Higgins and Linton, 2004; Janas et al., 2003; Abele and Tampé, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and inference from experimental results.

claim: It remains an open question whether a single ATP-binding-induced conformational switch drives substrate translocation in the case of fully functional wild-type ABC transporters.
source: To date, however, it remains an open question whether a single ATP-binding-induced conformational switch drives substrate translocation in the case of fully functional wild-type ABC transporters.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The relevance of futile ATP hydrolysis cycles as well as factors contributing to energy coupling (ratio of consumed ATP per translocated substrate) have remained unexplained for wild-type TmrAB and other ABC systems.
